subject: physics

items.q: (HT only) How can radio waves be produced?
items.correct: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
items.misconception: By heating a metal aerial till it glows
items.why: Emission by hot objects is the only production mechanism many students have met, so it is transferred to the radio part of the spectrum, where the real mechanism is an oscillating circuit. For radio waves the specification names one production mechanism: oscillations in electrical circuits.
items.random_wrong: By changes in the nucleus of the atom

items.q: (HT only) A radio wave is absorbed by an aerial joined to a circuit. What may the wave create in that circuit?
items.correct: An alternating current in that circuit
items.misconception: A steady direct current, always one way
items.why: Students associate 'a current is produced' with cells and steady flow, and the idea of a current that reverses millions of times a second is unfamiliar. The specification states that absorbed radio waves may create an alternating current, which is exactly why they can induce oscillations in a circuit.
items.random_wrong: A magnetic field but no current in it

items.q: (HT only) A transmitter sends out radio waves at 200 MHz. A receiving aerial absorbs them and an alternating current is created in the circuit joined to it. What is the frequency of that current?
items.correct: 200 MHz, the same as that radio wave
items.misconception: 100 MHz, half the frequency of the wave
items.why: Students expect a conversion between wave and current to change the number, by analogy with gears, transformers or the doubling they see in wave diagrams. The specification is explicit: the alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself.
items.random_wrong: 400 MHz, twice the frequency of the wave

items.correct: In changes in the nucleus of an atom
items.misconception: In changes to the electrons of an atom
items.why: Students meet electron energy changes as the source of light long before they meet gamma rays, so they extend the picture they already hold to every high-energy wave. Diagrams of atoms also draw the eye to the electrons rather than to the nucleus. Changes in atoms and in their nuclei can both produce electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, but the specification names the nucleus specifically as the origin of gamma rays.
items.random_wrong: In bonds being broken between two atoms

items.q: Which statement about how electromagnetic waves are generated and absorbed is correct?
items.correct: Changes in atoms and in their nuclei generate and absorb them
items.misconception: Only changes in the nuclei of atoms can generate these waves
items.why: Having learned the memorable fact that gamma rays come from the nucleus, students over-apply it and treat the nucleus as the source of all radiation. The specification says changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can result in waves over a wide frequency range. The nucleus is singled out only for gamma rays.
items.random_wrong: Only changes in the electrons of an atom can generate them

items.q: A worker's radiation dose is recorded in sieverts (Sv). What does this dose measure?
items.correct: The risk of harm that results from the exposure
items.misconception: The number of nuclei decaying near the worker
items.why: The word 'dose' is met first in medicine, where it means an amount of a substance, so students read it as an amount rather than as a measure of risk. Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure, not a count of decays and not a mass of material.
items.random_wrong: The amount of radioactive material in the body

items.q: Ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays can have hazardous effects on human body tissue. What do those effects depend on?
items.correct: The type of radiation and the size of the dose
items.misconception: The size of the dose received, whatever type it is
items.why: A single number in sieverts looks like the whole story, so students treat dose as the only variable and ignore the type of radiation named alongside it. The specification says the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose — both of them, not one.
items.random_wrong: Only the total size of the dose, not its type

items.q: A patient receives a radiation dose of 75 mSv from a scan. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). What is this dose in sieverts?
items.why: The prefix milli is confused with centi, and 100 is the conversion students use most often elsewhere, for example between metres and centimetres or in percentages. Milli means one thousandth. The specification gives the relationship directly: 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv).

items.q: The table shows the average dose a person in the UK receives each year: radon gas 1.3 mSv, medical X-rays 0.4 mSv, cosmic rays 0.3 mSv. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: Radon gives a larger yearly dose than the other two added
items.misconception: Medical X-rays give the largest yearly dose of the three
items.why: Everyday warnings about microwave ovens and mobile phones, and dramatic accounts of radiation from space, make students rank danger by familiarity or by how exotic the source is rather than by the specification's two factors. The specification names ultraviolet waves, X-rays and gamma rays as the ones that can have hazardous effects, and says the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose.
items.random_wrong: The three sources together give a dose of over one sievert

items.q: Three workers received yearly doses of 6 mSv, 18 mSv and 0.5 Sv. Use 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). Which worker is at the greatest risk of harm?
items.correct: The worker on 0.5 Sv, because that equals 500 mSv
items.misconception: The worker on 18 mSv, the largest number shown
items.why: Students compare the digits in a table without first checking that the units in the column are the same, and 0.5 looks small next to 18. Convert everything to one unit first, using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv. Then 0.5 Sv becomes 500 mSv, far larger than 18 mSv.
items.random_wrong: The worker on 6 mSv, since small doses build up most

items.q: What effects can ultraviolet waves have on human body tissue?
items.correct: Skin ages early and the risk of skin cancer rises
items.misconception: Genes mutate, as ultraviolet is ionising radiation
items.why: All three are grouped together as hazardous in the same sentence of the specification, so students merge them and give ultraviolet the mechanism named for the other two. The specification names X-rays and gamma rays as the ionising radiations that mutate genes; for ultraviolet it names premature ageing of the skin and an increased risk of skin cancer.
items.random_wrong: Skin ages early but the risk of cancer is unchanged

items.q: Why can X-rays and gamma rays cause cancer in human body tissue?
items.correct: They are ionising and can cause genes to mutate
items.misconception: They are absorbed by the skin and make it age early
items.why: Premature ageing of skin is taught as a hazard of ultraviolet, and sunlight damage is the most familiar radiation harm, so students transfer this surface skin effect to every high-energy electromagnetic wave. Premature skin ageing is a hazard of ultraviolet. X-rays and gamma rays penetrate deep into body tissue; because they are ionising they can mutate genes and cause cancer, not surface ageing.
items.random_wrong: They heat body cells until those cells are killed

items.q: A dose is 75 mSv. What is it in sieverts?
items.misconception: The number is left unchanged, so 75 mSv is written as 75 Sv.
items.why: Under time pressure students copy the number across and change only the unit, especially when the prefix milli is unfamiliar in a new context. 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv), so a dose in mSv must be divided by 1000 to give a dose in sieverts.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What can ultraviolet waves do to the human body?
items.correct: Ultraviolet waves can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer.
items.misconception: Ultraviolet only ages the skin, by heating it; the risk of cancer comes from X-rays and gamma rays alone.
items.why: Sunburn feels like heat, so students explain ultraviolet damage as heating, and they reserve cancer for the radiations they have been told are ionising. The specification names two effects of ultraviolet on the body: skin ageing prematurely and an increased risk of skin cancer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A worker receives a radiation dose of a few millisieverts. Is there any risk of harm?
items.correct: Yes, a small risk. Radiation dose in sieverts is a measure of the risk of harm, and the risk grows as the dose grows — it does not switch off at small doses.
items.misconception: Small radiation doses are completely safe, so all workers on small-sounding doses face the same zero risk.
items.why: Everyday limits such as speed limits and alcohol guidelines suggest a threshold below which nothing matters, so students treat every dose that sounds small as equally harmless instead of comparing the doses. Dose in sieverts measures the risk of harm: the larger the dose, the larger the risk. Doses must be compared in the same unit — 0.5 Sv is 500 mSv, far larger than 6 mSv or 18 mSv, so that worker is at the greatest risk.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.2.3 Properties of electromagnetic waves 2
